\chapter{Green and Yellow}
\label{ch:ar-green-and-yellow}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name green and yellow in Arabic and trace aṣfar to the same root as ṣifr, 'zero'.}

Say akhḍar beside khuḍār, 'vegetables', then aṣfar beside ṣifr, and follow ṣifr into English zero and cipher.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{أخضر}, \ar{أصفر}]{\ar{أخضر}, \ar{أصفر} — \textquotedblleft{}greens\textquotedblright{} you'd recognize, and a hidden zero}

\label{lesson:AR-C22-akhdar-asfar}



\begin{quote}
Arabic's green word hides an English-style pun. Its yellow word hides something even better — the exact root behind the word \textquotedblleft{}zero\textquotedblright{} itself.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ar{أخضر}} (\emph{akhḍar}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{green}\textquotedblright{}) comes from the root \textbf{\ar{خ}-\ar{ض}-\ar{ر}} (\emph{kh-ḍ-r}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to be green}\textquotedblright{}). That same root gives \textbf{\ar{خضار}} (\emph{khuḍār}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{vegetables}\textquotedblright{}) — echoing the exact same move English makes when it calls vegetables \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{greens}.\textquotedblright{} The same root also names the mysterious Quranic figure \textbf{\ar{الخِضْر}} (\emph{al-Khiḍr}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the Green One}\textquotedblright{} — traditionally said to be called this because the ground turned green wherever he sat or prayed.
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
Here's the real surprise: \textbf{\ar{أصفر}} (\emph{aṣfar}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{yellow}\textquotedblright{}) shares its root, \textbf{\ar{ص}-\ar{ف}-\ar{ر}} (\emph{ṣ-f-r}), with \textbf{\ar{صفر}} (\emph{ṣifr}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{zero, empty, void}\textquotedblright{}) — the \textbf{exact} Arabic word that gave English both \textbf{zero} (via Italian \emph{zefiro}/\emph{zero}) and \textbf{cipher} (via Medieval Latin \emph{cifra}). So the same three-letter Arabic root sits behind \textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{} and behind the number \textbf{zero} itself. The sources don't fully explain \emph{why} \textquotedblleft{}emptiness\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{} share a root — but the shared root itself, connecting Arabic's yellow-word straight back to the origin of \textquotedblleft{}zero,\textquotedblright{} is genuine and well documented.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}akhḍar\textquotedblright{} — green, same root as \textquotedblleft{}khuḍār,\textquotedblright{} vegetables
  \item \textquotedblleft{}aṣfar\textquotedblright{} — yellow, same root as \textquotedblleft{}ṣifr,\textquotedblright{} zero
  \item the connection — \textquotedblleft{}aṣfar, ṣifr, zero, cipher\textquotedblright{} — one Arabic root, reaching all the way into English math vocabulary
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root does \textbf{\ar{أخضر}} share with \textquotedblleft{}vegetables,\textquotedblright{} and what English phrase does this echo? (\textbf{\ar{خ}-\ar{ض}-\ar{ر}}, \emph{kh-ḍ-r} — echoes English calling vegetables \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{greens}.\textquotedblright{}) What Quranic figure shares this root, and what does his name mean? (\textbf{\ar{الخِضْر}}, \emph{al-Khiḍr} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the Green One}.\textquotedblright{}) What word does \textbf{\ar{أصفر}} share its root with, and what two English words trace back to it? (\textbf{\ar{صفر}}, \emph{ṣifr}, \textquotedblleft{}zero, empty\textquotedblright{} — the source of English \textbf{zero} and \textbf{cipher}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
